title: VersionRAG: Version-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Evolving Documents
research_question: Can retrieval-augmented generation explicitly represent document versions and changes so that questions about historical content, version identity, and inter-version differences are answered more accurately and efficiently than version-agnostic RAG?
methodology: VersionRAG represents evolving documentation as a five-level graph containing category, document, version, content, and change nodes, with temporal links between versions and explicit or automatically derived change information. A query classifier routes content, version, and change questions to specialized retrieval procedures over Neo4j and Milvus Lite, while DeepDiff is used to derive implicit line-level changes when changelogs are unavailable. The authors construct VersionQA with 100 manually curated questions over 34 technical-documentation files and compare VersionRAG against naive vector RAG and Neo4j GraphRAG using Llama 3 8B, GPT-4o Mini, and DeepSeek-R1 70B. GPT-4.1 grades answers against gold references, and the complete set of 100 answers is also manually reviewed.

key_findings.finding: With DeepSeek-R1 70B, VersionRAG achieved 90% overall accuracy on VersionQA, compared with 58% for naive RAG and 64% for the evaluated GraphRAG baseline.

VersionRAG achieved 100% accuracy on the evaluated version-specific content retrieval and version-listing categories with the strongest evaluated model, showing a large advantage on questions that require explicit version identity.

Change-oriented questions remained substantially harder than ordinary content or version questions; the strongest configuration reached 70% change-query accuracy, with implicit changes particularly difficult.

For DeepSeek-R1 70B, VersionRAG used about 186K input tokens and 38K output tokens compared with roughly 2.97M input and 5.92M output tokens for GraphRAG, corresponding to the paper's reported 97% token reduction and substantially lower cost and runtime.
The reported VersionRAG failures were attributed mainly to query misclassification and incomplete change extraction, demonstrating error propagation across the modular pipeline.

The evaluation does not establish that VersionRAG's gains generalize from the small technical-documentation benchmark to domains such as legal, medical, financial, or heterogeneous workplace documents.

limitations: VersionQA contains only 100 questions over 34 technical-documentation files, limiting evidence for cross-domain generalization.
Implicit semantic changes remain difficult: the strongest reported configuration obtains only 60% accuracy on implicit-change questions.
Line-level DeepDiff can miss semantically important changes that are not well represented by textual diffs.

The system assumes that version information can be extracted reliably and that document versions have sufficiently consistent structure; irregular filenames, date-based schemes, or missing metadata can cause failures.
The graph models versions primarily as a sequential history and does not directly represent arbitrary branching, merging, or non-adjacent version dependencies.
Accuracy depends strongly on the underlying LLM; smaller models create fewer useful change nodes and misclassify more queries.
The architecture requires both graph and vector infrastructure and still incurs nontrivial indexing cost.
The pipeline has no end-to-end mechanism that corrects errors introduced by version extraction, change extraction, or query routing.
raw_claims: VersionRAG explicitly stores individual document versions rather than flattening all versions into a common retrieval collection.
Its hierarchy separates documents, versions, version content, and changes between versions.
Queries are classified into content, version, or change-oriented retrieval paths.
VersionQA contains 100 manually curated questions drawn from versioned technical documentation.
Sixty percent of the benchmark questions are version-sensitive.
Naive RAG and the evaluated GraphRAG baseline perform substantially worse than VersionRAG on the complete benchmark with the strongest tested model.
Questions asking about implicit changes are harder than questions supported by explicit changelogs.
The version-aware graph allows retrieved information to retain provenance to a particular version.
VersionRAG requires far fewer indexing-generation tokens than the evaluated GraphRAG pipeline.
Misclassification and incomplete change extraction account for the reported VersionRAG failures.
The authors publicly provide the VersionRAG code and VersionQA dataset.
